evidence: per size (costs do not vary within a size)
limits: A count is not a time. Operations and depth are an accounting convention over shapes and data dependencies on an idealised machine of P identical processors (no communication, synchronisation, load imbalance or memory contention), exactly reproducible by anyone, so they can show 'A can be made faster than B once there are enough processors' and cannot show how fast either runs on any real device. Depth is a conservative bound: per-tensor granularity and the host rule can only overstate it. The ladder is the prover's unless it was fixed in advance.
a positive gap means A's critical path is the smaller: 1 bit is half, 3 bits an eighth
instances a solver did not solve are left out of the gap and counted separately; if one solver fails where the other solves, that failure is not in the bits

a size where both solvers cost exactly the same on every instance (a fixed number of steps) is one exact fact about that size, not many samples: it carries no p-value, and nothing is said about sizes that were not measured
the sign test and the bootstrap interval use only the sizes where costs vary between instances

span is the depth of the tensor operations plus the solver's own Python instructions, one for one (they run one after another): it is the length of the critical path of an idealised machine, so the operations gap beside it matters, because a shorter path is usually bought with more total work

the processor counts compare each run's exact work, depth and Python steps on an idealised machine of identical processors (Brent's bounds): no communication, synchronisation, load imbalance or memory contention is modelled, and 'certainly faster' means every machine the model covers, not any real device
the ladders used the public practice seed, so the hidden parts of every instance (the teacher and the test set) can be computed by anyone: this shows the method, not a certified result
the ladders were not required to match a plan committed in advance (--plan), so the sizes and instances were the prover's choice
the ladders were checked for internal consistency and EVERY record of all three was re-executed here with identical counts

parallel.statement: A is certainly faster than B at every measured size from 512 processor(s) up (A's upper bound below B's lower bound), and B is not, below it; at 1 processor B is certainly faster instead

verdict: A used a shorter critical path than B at every measured size (4); but that side did 1.56x more total operations: a shorter critical path is bought with extra work, so it wins only with enough processors (see the processor counts below, computed exactly from the work and the span)
